meta.label: Reusable nappies
tradeoffLabels: cheapest over two and a half years
meta.attribution: Prices are quoted from each brand's own site on the date shown, for a single nappy or the stated bundle; nobody's actual cost depends only on unit price, since a full-time cloth user needs a stock of 15 to 25 nappies to get through laundry cycles, so figures that state a full-supply cost (GroVia, Little Lamb, Mother-ease) are noted separately from single-item prices. The environment score for every system leans on the UK Environment Agency's 2008 updated lifecycle assessment of nappies, which found that a reusable nappy's manufacture matters less than how it is washed and dried: its baseline scenario put reusable nappies at about the same carbon footprint as a 2006 disposable, full loads and line-drying cut that by up to 40 percent below disposables, and washing at 90C plus tumble-drying every load raised it as much as 75 percent above the baseline. That study did not test individual brands, so scores here describe how a system's fabric and design (bulkier bamboo fitteds dry slower than thin cotton prefolds; a hybrid that is washed less often per change uses less water) interact with that same laundering evidence, not an independent test of the brand itself. Entries added in 2026-10 also draw on the Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide, which summarises Defra's newer 2023 life cycle assessment: it found reusables produce about 25 percent less CO2 than disposables over two and a half years but more impact from washing and drying, and recommends line-drying; each nappy's own care instructions are read against that. A laundry service is scored on cost and ease only, because no service checked publishes its laundering footprint. Disposable nappies are a separate decision in this catalogue. Not medical or safety advice. Reviewed 2026-08; additions checked 2026-10. Suggest changes via Contribute.

criteria.label: Cost per nappy or full supply

products.name: TotsBots Bamboozle (fitted + wrap)

economical.note: TotsBots' own store now lists the Bamboozle nappy, the absorbent inner, at $15.99 but marks every colour and size as sold out or unavailable; the page says it works when 'teamed up with the matching bamboozle waterproof wraps', sold separately, so the price does not cover a full change even when stock returns.

accessibility.note: Companies House shows the original maker, Tots Bots Limited (SC254962), went into court winding-up in December 2023 and was dissolved on 22 July 2026. The TotsBots site is still live but its contact page says the products are currently being manufactured and refers UK and EU trade buyers to distributors, with nothing in stock in its store when checked, so a family cannot currently buy it new from the brand. In use it is also a two-part fitted-and-wrap system, an extra step at every change compared with an all-in-one.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. A bulky bamboo fitted nappy like this one takes longer to line-dry than a thin cotton prefold, so a household relying on a tumble dryer for it sits toward the higher-impact end of that finding.

products.description: A two-part bamboo fitted nappy and wrap system from a Glasgow brand whose original company was wound up and dissolved; the brand's site says production is restarting, but nothing was in stock when checked.

products.name: GroVia O.N.E.

economical.note: GroVia's own product page prices the O.N.E. at $24.95 each and states plainly that for full-time use 'you will spend between $550 - $600' on a complete supply, one of the few brands here to give a total cost rather than only a unit price.

accessibility.note: The page describes a 'modular snap in no-prep soaker system' built into a single all-in-one shell, closer to a disposable's one-piece use than a two-part fitted-and-wrap system, though the page also recommends washing every two days.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. GroVia lists a polyester microfiber hidden inner layer and a polyester-microfleece-topped cotton soaker, synthetic fabrics rather than plain cotton or bamboo; the finding that washing and drying drive most of the in-use footprint applies regardless of fabric.

products.description: A one-piece hybrid nappy with swap-in soaker pads; GroVia's own page is unusual in stating a full two-and-a-half-year supply cost outright rather than leaving buyers to work it out.

products.name: Charlie Banana 2-in-1

economical.note: Charlie Banana's own collection page lists reusable cloth diapers from $11.99 to $129.99 depending on pack size and design; the shell is reused across many changes, with only the insert changed each time.

accessibility.note: The brand's own page states 'you can choose between our washable, reusable inserts or opt for disposable inserts for quick and easy cleanups, all using the same diaper shell cover,' letting a household switch to near-disposable convenience for outings or childcare without buying a second system.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. With its reusable insert this system carries the same wash-and-dry-driven footprint; switching to the brand's disposable insert for some changes cuts laundering but brings back single-use waste for those changes.

products.description: A reusable shell that takes either a washable insert or a disposable one, giving a household the option to fall back to disposable-level convenience without switching systems.

products.name: ALVABABY pocket nappy

economical.note: ALVABABY's own product page lists its one-size solid-colour pocket diaper at $5.69, the cheapest single branded nappy in this comparison by a wide margin.

accessibility.note: The page describes a 'pocket design' that must be stuffed with an insert before use, an extra step compared with an all-in-one, and a polyester outer with 'faux suede cloth inside' that the page says draws moisture away; no washing or drying guidance is given on the page.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. The shell is polyester with a TPU waterproof layer, a synthetic construction, and the product page discloses no third-party certification or washing guidance.

products.description: An imported budget pocket nappy, by far the cheapest branded single nappy here, with no third-party certification disclosed on its own product page.

products.name: Disana wool cover

economical.note: Green Mountain Diapers lists the Disana Wool Pull-On Cover, made by Disana in Germany, at $42.95 for most sizes; a wool cover is worn over a separate absorbent layer, so this price does not include the nappy itself.

accessibility.note: The retailer's page for this Disana cover says 'HAND WASH AND FLAT DRY ONLY. Do not put it in the dryer,' and that it must be felted by hand before first use, more manual effort per wash than any machine-washable system in this comparison, even though washing itself is needed only rarely.

environment.note: The same page states wool covers need washing only infrequently, 'sometimes only once a month,' far below the weekly-or-more wash cycle the Environment Agency study assumed for shaped nappies and wraps, so the electricity and water use per month is much lower even before accounting for hand-washing instead of a machine.

products.description: A merino wool cover worn over a separate absorbent nappy; it needs washing only about once a month, but every wash is by hand, and it is one more purchase on top of the nappy underneath it.

products.name: Cloth-eez prefold + cover

economical.note: Green Mountain Diapers lists a dozen Cloth-eez prefold diapers at a sale price of $32.95, or about $2.75 each; the page notes this is 'the inner absorbent part of the diaper system' and 'requires a cover (sold separately),' so the true per-change cost is higher once a cover is added.

accessibility.note: The page describes '100% cotton exclusive of trim' in a '4-8-4 ply' construction that must be folded and fastened, then paired with a separate waterproof cover, the most hands-on system in this comparison alongside terry squares.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. A thin, unbleached cotton prefold like this one dries far faster on a line than a bulky fitted or all-in-one nappy, which suits the line-drying the guide recommends; the retailer also describes it as chlorine-free and OEKO-TEX 100 certified.

products.description: The traditional folded-cotton nappy, cheapest per piece of any absorbent layer in this comparison, but the most fiddly to use and sold without the cover it needs.

products.name: Esembly Inner + Outer bundle

economical.note: Esembly's own site prices its organic cloth diaper starter bundle, an Inner and an Outer, at $57.

accessibility.note: The product page describes the Inner as having 'built-in snaps for fast, foolproof closure' paired with a waterproof Outer, and states 'machine drying recommended,' a simpler routine than the hand-wash-only or fold-and-pin systems in this comparison.

environment.note: Esembly's page states the Inner is '100% unbleached Organic Cotton' and the Outer is '100% GRS certified upcycled polyester TPU (derived from recycled plastic bottles),' both OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified; recommending machine drying rather than requiring it leaves room for the line-drying practice the Environment Agency study found most beneficial.

products.description: An organic-cotton inner paired with a recycled-plastic waterproof outer, both independently certified, at a mid-range price for a starter bundle rather than a single nappy.

products.name: Pop-in All-in-Two

economical.note: Close Parent's own collection page prices Pop-in All-in-Two bamboo nappies between £10.99 and £22.55 per nappy; because the waterproof shell separates from the absorbent part and is reused across several changes before it needs washing, fewer shells are needed than in a system where the whole nappy is washed every time.

accessibility.note: The page describes the nappy and wrap as 'connected, but you can take them apart,' an all-in-two design meant to combine the convenience of an all-in-one with the ability to reuse the shell, closer to disposable-style ease than a fully separate two-part system.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. The guide also notes that with two-part nappies the outer wrap only needs changing about every 12 hours unless soiled; the Pop-in's separable shell works the same way, so fewer pieces go through the wash than with a nappy washed whole every time, though its bamboo layer dries more slowly than thin cotton.

products.description: A bamboo all-in-two nappy whose waterproof shell separates from the absorbent part and can be reused for more than one change, cutting the number of wash loads needed.

products.name: Little Lamb day and night complete kit

economical.note: Little Lamb's own product page lists this complete kit, 15 one-size pocket nappies, 10 bamboo fitted nappies, 5 wraps, a nappy pail, a wet bag, boosters, wipes and liners, at a regular price of £594.00 and a sale price of £415.00, one of the few full two-and-a-half-year supply prices stated outright in this comparison.

accessibility.note: The kit combines one-size pocket nappies with fitted nappies and includes a nappy pail and wet bag, so a household does not need to separately research and buy those pieces; the page's own washing guidance calls for 'a full, long cycle at 40 or 60 degrees.'

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide summarises Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, which found 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' over the first two and a half years, but with more impact than disposables in other areas, mainly from the electricity used to wash and tumble dry; it advises line-drying. Little Lamb's own kit page recommends line drying in direct sunshine, or near but not touching a radiator, which matches that advice, though the kit's bamboo fitted nappies dry more slowly than a thin cotton prefold.

products.description: A turnkey day-and-night kit combining pocket and fitted nappies with the pail and wet bag a household would otherwise buy separately, priced as a full two-and-a-half-year supply rather than per nappy.

products.name: Secondhand cloth nappies

economical.note: The charity NCT's own page on its Nearly New Sales, which it says help parents sell and recycle 'over 200,000 preloved items every year,' describes buyers picking up secondhand baby and children's essentials at 'around a quarter to a third of the price' of buying new; the page does not price cloth nappies specifically, but nappies are among the reusable baby goods commonly resold through this and similar secondhand channels.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 reusable nappy guide reports Defra's 2023 finding that 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' and that reusing nappies for a second child could cut their climate change impact by 6.5 percent and water use by 30.9 percent, because the manufacturing impact is spread across more use; buying a nappy secondhand from another family works the same way, since its manufacturing footprint has already been spent.

products.description: Buying used cloth nappies through a resale marketplace, a nearly-new sale, or a swap group; condition and hygiene depend entirely on the seller, which no score here can capture.

products.name: Cloth nappy library or trial kit

economical.note: Real Nappies for London's own page on cloth nappy libraries says they let a family 'try before you buy' and that 'most offer nappy kit loans on a monthly or weekly basis, some even offer long term loans,' run mostly by volunteers who are parents with experience of cloth nappies; the page does not state a loan fee, but describes loan kits rather than a purchase.

products.description: Borrowing a trial kit from a volunteer-run nappy library before buying anything, so a family can compare fitted, pocket and all-in-one systems on their own baby first. A loan, not a permanent supply, so it does not replace choosing and buying a system.

products.name: Council reusable nappy voucher or laundry service subsidy

economical.note: Real Nappies for London's own site states residents in participating boroughs can 'claim a voucher worth up to £70 to help with the upfront cost of buying reusable nappies or put towards a washable nappy laundry service'; other UK councils outside London run comparable schemes, but eligibility and amounts vary by local authority and this scheme is limited to specific London boroughs.

accessibility.note: Because the same voucher can be put toward a nappy laundry service instead of nappies themselves, a family can pay someone else to collect and wash dirty nappies weekly, removing the laundering step the Environment Agency study identified as the main driver of a reusable nappy's cost and effort in use, though only where a participating laundry service operates.

products.description: A council voucher that offsets the cost of buying any of the systems above, or that can instead pay toward a weekly nappy laundry service so a household does not do the washing itself; available only in some UK local authority areas.

products.name: Smart Bottoms Smart One 4.0 (all-in-one)

economical.note: Smart Bottoms' own product page prices the one-size Smart One 4.0 at $28.00, slightly more than the GroVia O.N.E. here; at the 15 to 25 nappies a full-time user needs, that is roughly $420 to $700 before any covers or extras, since this nappy needs none.

accessibility.note: The page describes a true all-in-one: 'No stuffing, snapping, or assembling required', with a folding attached insert and a one-size fit from 10 to 35 pounds, and says 'Most machines will fully dry the diaper in one warm cycle', the closest thing to a disposable among the cotton nappies here.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide, summarising Defra's 2023 life cycle assessment, says 'reusable nappies produce 25% less CO2 than single-use disposable nappies' but warns of 'Higher water and energy usage from frequent washing' and advises line-drying rather than tumble drying; the Smart One has a certified organic cotton inner and a TPU outer, and its own care label says wash warm and dry warm, a routine that leans on the tumble dryer.

products.description: A one-size organic cotton all-in-one with nothing to assemble, at a mid-range price per nappy; its care label assumes machine drying.

products.name: Mother-ease Element fitted full-time package

economical.note: Mother-ease's own page prices its Element Fitted Full-Time Package at $643.99 for 24 one-size cotton terry fitted nappies, 10 one-size snap covers and 2 boosters, described as everything needed for a complete system from 8 to 35 pounds; that is a stated full-supply price, a little above GroVia's own $550 to $600 estimate.

accessibility.note: The package is a two-part system: the page says to use the fitted nappies alone under 6 months, add the snap-in liner after that, and lay in a booster for naps and nights, all under a separate cover, an extra step at every change compared with an all-in-one.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide reports Defra's 2023 finding that reusables carry about 25 percent less CO2 than disposables but more impact from washing and drying, and advises line-drying; Mother-ease's own wash guide calls for a full cycle using hot water at the highest water level, then line or tumble drying, a hotter routine than the 40 degree washes other brands here recommend. Mother-ease also says its Ontario factory has bought 100 percent green electricity since 2007.

products.description: A Canadian-made cotton fitted-and-cover system sold to the US and Canada as a complete full-time package with a stated total price; its wash guide calls for hot water.

products.name: Blueberry One Size Simplex (organic cotton)

economical.note: Blueberry's own product page lists the One Size Simplex in Organic Cotton at $28.99, with many prints marked sold out at the time of checking; the site was running a 20 percent sitewide sale.

accessibility.note: The page describes 'An all-in-one diaper design that combines the convenience of an all-in-one diaper while providing the absorbency adjustability of a pocket diaper', with half the soaker attached and pocket openings at both ends so extra inserts can be added and wash out on their own.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide summarises Defra's 2023 finding that washing and drying drive most of a reusable nappy's impact and advises line-drying; the Simplex combines a 100 percent organic cotton inner with a polyester waterproof outer and a polyester stay-dry layer, and Blueberry's own care note asks for a warm prep wash up to 140F, without saying how to dry it.

products.description: A US-made organic cotton all-in-one with pocket openings for extra absorbency, at about the same single-nappy price as the other all-in-ones here.

products.name: Kit & Kin reusable cloth nappy

economical.note: Kit & Kin's own page lists its one-size all-in-one reusable nappy at £17.99, down from £19.99, but showed it out of stock in all three designs when checked; the Which? February 2026 guide separately notes Boots sells Kit & Kin reusables at up to £20.

accessibility.note: The page describes a one-size all-in-one with hook-and-loop tabs and adjustable poppers from 8 pounds, with an attached gusset that tucks in for washing, and says 'We recommend machine washing at 40 degrees with a non-bio powder' on a long cycle, a simple routine though hook-and-loop must be fastened before every wash.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide reports that Defra's 2023 assessment found reusables produce about 25 percent less CO2 than disposables and advises 'line-drying nappies rather than tumble drying' to save energy; Kit & Kin's own care guidance matches, recommending air drying and a cool tumble only, with a TENCEL and hemp inner and a recycled polyester outer.

products.description: A one-size all-in-one from a UK B Corp nappy brand, with a TENCEL and hemp inner and a 40 degree, air-dry care routine; out of stock on the brand's own site when checked.

products.name: Healthybaby Our Cloth Diaper Bundle

economical.note: Healthybaby's own page prices its cloth bundle at $90 for three organic cotton inner diapers, one waterproof outer cover and one overnight liner; it comes in Small, Medium and Large rather than one size, so a family buys again as the baby grows.

accessibility.note: The Which? February 2026 guide describes two-part nappies as a separate inner nappy and outer wrap, and notes that with sized rather than one-size nappies a family has to buy new ones as the baby grows; Healthybaby's bundle is both, buttoned inner diapers under a separate cover in Small, Medium and Large from 6 to 35 pounds, so it takes more steps and more re-buying than a one-size all-in-one.

environment.note: Healthybaby's page says the inner diapers are 'Made of 100% unbleached, GOTS Certified Organic Cotton' and the cover is OEKO-TEX certified REPREVE fabric made from recycled plastic bottles, close to the certified organic-and-recycled materials of the Esembly bundle here; like every reusable, its real footprint depends on how it is washed and dried.

products.description: An organic cotton inner-and-cover bundle from the brand behind an EWG Verified disposable, sold in three sizes rather than one-size.

products.name: Bambino Mio Mio Solo (all-in-one)

economical.note: London nappy shop Nappy Ever After lists the Bambino Mio Mio Solo at £13.00; the Which? February 2026 guide says Ocado usually sells Bambino Mio nappies at £16 and sometimes as little as £10. Bambino Mio's own website was offline for updates when checked and pointed buyers to retailers.

accessibility.note: The retailer's product page describes a one-piece all-in-one with 'no extra parts' that 'Fits from around 3 months to potty training', with an inside pocket for extra inserts; it is not designed to fit a newborn.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide reports Defra's 2023 finding that washing and drying drive most of a reusable nappy's impact and advises line-drying; the retailer's page says the Mio Solo has a stay-dry layer and is OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified but does not give its fabrics, and a stay-dry all-in-one generally dries more slowly on a line than a two-part cotton system.

products.description: A long-running UK all-in-one sold through supermarkets and nappy shops; Bambino Mio's own site was offline when checked, so price and description come from a retailer.

products.name: Nappy laundry service (Nappy Ever After, London)

economical.note: Nappy Ever After's own page says 'The service costs £15.00 per week for the hire, delivery, collection and laundering of the nappies', about £720 over 48 paid weeks a year, plus wraps; a council voucher can offset the start, and its starter-kit page shows a £54.15 Real Nappies for London voucher taking the first month to £38. Over two and a half years that is more than the roughly £1,000 Which? cites for leading-brand disposables.

accessibility.note: Real Nappies for London's own page on laundry services says three London services deliver clean cotton nappies weekly and take dirty ones away to be professionally laundered, 'For a weekly payment ranging between £12 and £20 depending on the service'; only the waterproof wraps are washed at home, which removes the laundry step that makes cloth harder than disposables. Coverage is limited to parts of London.

links.label: Real Nappies for London: laundry services

products.description: A weekly collect-and-deliver cotton nappy service in parts of London, the most disposable-like way to use cloth and also the most expensive over time; laundering footprint is not scored because none of the services publishes it.

products.name: Mama Koala Pocket Diaper 3.0 (6-pack with inserts)

economical.note: Mama Koala's own store lists a six-pack of its one-size Pocket Diaper 3.0 with six bamboo-polyester inserts at $42.99, about $7.17 per nappy including its insert, among the cheapest complete nappies in this comparison alongside ALVABABY.

accessibility.note: The product description says each pocket nappy has an athletic wicking jersey lining, crossover snaps for a newborn fit and rise snaps for one size from 8 to 40 pounds; as a pocket design it has to be stuffed with its insert before use and unstuffed before washing, an extra step compared with an all-in-one.

environment.note: The Which? February 2026 guide, summarising Defra's 2023 assessment, says reusables still have lower carbon than disposables but warns of 'Higher water and energy usage from frequent washing' and advises line-drying; Mama Koala's nappies use a synthetic wicking jersey lining and 4-layer bamboo polyester inserts, and the product description gives no washing or drying guidance and no third-party certification.

products.description: A widely sold budget pocket nappy, bought in six-packs with inserts; cheap per nappy, with synthetic fabrics and no certification or care guidance in its product description.
